introHeading: Perceived objects and the minds that perceive
intro: This edition preserves five original prompts, the original “Quizzes” heading, and all three model response tracks. It follows the original sequence: influence, seven contributions, likely causes of prominence, fields of reception, three seven-question quizzes, and three twelve-question discussion lists. The responses distinguish Berkeley’s denial of material substance from denial of ordinary objects, and passive ideas from active spirits.
description: Examine Berkeley’s immaterialism, perception, abstraction, language, and reception through the original three response tracks and restored quizzes.
headings: How Berkeley changed the debate about perception
Three original selections of seven contributions
Reception across philosophy and the study of perception
Three sets of twelve discussion questions

pageSignals.Best for: distinguishing ideas, spirits, and material substance

replacements.1.1.1: George Berkeley (1685–1753) challenged the need for material substance underlying experience while defending the reality of ordinary perceived objects. His immaterialism distinguishes passive ideas from active perceiving spirits; “to be is to be perceived” applies to sensible things, not to spirits in the same way. This sharpened disputes about perception, abstraction, and skepticism. Hume explicitly praised his critique of abstract ideas, while Kant’s later engagement included resisting an identification of his own idealism with Berkeley’s.
replacements.1.2.1: Berkeley made empiricism confront a radical possibility: perhaps ordinary objects consist in perceived sensible qualities, without an unknowable material support behind them. His distinction between ideas and spirits prevents this from being a claim that only one person’s private images exist.
replacements.1.2.2: His work also asks how vision becomes connected with distance and touch, and how general words function without abstract mental pictures. These remain useful problems even for readers who reject his immaterialism and its appeal to God.
replacements.1.3.0: Berkeley’s immaterialism denies mind-independent material substance, not the tables, trees, and other sensible things of ordinary life. Ideas are perceived; spirits perceive and act. By combining that distinction with criticisms of abstraction and representational theories of perception, he gave later philosophers a demanding alternative to accounts in which experience merely copies a material world beyond it. The status of other minds, divine agency, and unobserved objects remains central to assessing the alternative.
replacements.2.1.5: Description: For sensible things, existence consists in being perceived. Berkeley does not infer that a room disappears whenever its human occupants leave: its continued existence belongs to a divine order independent of any one finite observer. Active spirits are not passive ideas to which the slogan applies unchanged.
replacements.2.1.8: Description: Berkeley rejects allegedly abstract ideas, such as a triangle that has no determinate shape. He does not deny general thought: a particular diagram or word can represent many instances without becoming an impossible indeterminate image.
replacements.2.1.11: Description: In Principles §§22–23, Berkeley challenges the reader to conceive a sensible object existing wholly unperceived. Imagining a tree with no nearby observer is still an act of thought. A critic can reply that the act of conceiving must be distinguished from what the imagined situation contains; the inference is contested.
replacements.2.1.12: Impact: The argument makes the relation between conceivability and existence explicit. Whether conceiving an unperceived object involves a contradiction is a question to examine, not a result secured simply by naming the “master argument.”
replacements.2.1.17: Description: Hume explicitly credits Berkeley’s treatment of general ideas in Treatise 1.1.7. Hume does not thereby accept Berkeley’s theology or his account of active spirits, so influence must be distinguished from agreement.
replacements.2.1.18: Impact: This supplies a specific link in the empiricist debate. Later responses, including Kant’s, should be read as distinct arguments rather than stages of one unchanged idealist doctrine.
replacements.2.2.1: The following seven entries preserve the original selection while clarifying what Berkeley argues and what remains disputed:
replacements.2.2.2: Immaterialism and “Esse est percipi”: Sensible objects consist in ideas perceived by minds rather than material supports outside all perception. Berkeley also recognizes active spirits, whose existence is not simply another instance of being perceived. He means to preserve ordinary things while rejecting a philosophical account of their supposed material substratum.
replacements.2.2.3: Critique of Material Substance: Berkeley challenges the intelligibility and explanatory need of an unperceived material support for sensible qualities. He does not reject substance altogether: spirits remain active substances in his system. His opponents’ material-substance theories should not be confused with the claim that everything, including minds, is material.
replacements.2.2.4: A New Theory of Vision: Berkeley argues that distance is not immediately seen. Through experience, visual signs become associated with tangible distance and movement. This is not necessarily a conscious geometrical inference, nor is it a complete modern scientific account of vision; it is a historically important theory about learning relations between the senses.
replacements.2.2.5: Mind and the External World: Sensory ideas occur independently of an individual’s will and display regular order. Berkeley appeals to an active divine cause and a world sustained independently of finite observers. “God keeps looking” is a useful shorthand only if it does not turn divine knowledge into a larger version of human passive sensation.
replacements.2.2.6: Language and Meaning: Berkeley rejects the requirement that every significant word must summon a distinct idea on every use. General signs can stand for particulars, and speech can prompt action or feeling as well as communicate ideas. His Principles, Introduction §§18–20, therefore contradicts the source’s claim that words mean something only by naming mental images.
replacements.2.2.7: The Problem of Skepticism: Berkeley tries to remove the gap between immediately perceived objects and allegedly inaccessible material originals. He does not make every skeptical problem irrelevant: questions about other spirits, sensory order, and his appeal to God still require argument. The claim that doubting implies a doubter is not his full response.
replacements.2.2.8: Empiricism and the Limits of Knowledge: Berkeley gives sense experience a central role, but also distinguishes knowledge of ideas from our notion of active spirit. Saying that every kind of knowledge is simply a sensory idea would erase a distinction his system needs. His disagreements with Locke take place within empiricist inquiry rather than outside it.
replacements.2.2.9: These arguments connect perception, ontology, and language without making them interchangeable. The difficult question is whether rejecting material substance explains experience more successfully or shifts the explanatory burden onto spirits and God.
replacements.2.3.1: Subjective Idealism/Immaterialism: Ordinary sensible objects are collections of ideas rather than mind-independent material substances. Calling the view “subjective” must not imply that everything depends on one human observer or is voluntarily invented.
replacements.2.3.2: Critique of Abstract Ideas: Berkeley rejects indeterminate abstract images while allowing particular ideas and words to function generally. Denying such images is not denying that we can reason about triangles or people in general.
replacements.2.3.3: Critique of Material Substance: He challenges an unperceived material support behind sensible qualities. His argument leaves active spiritual substance in place, so it is not a rejection of every kind of substance.
replacements.2.3.4: “To be is to be perceived”: This concerns sensible ideas and objects. Spirits instead perceive and act; the slogan is not an undifferentiated definition of the existence of everything.
replacements.2.3.5: Role of God: Divine agency and knowledge explain, within Berkeley’s system, an ordered world independent of an individual’s attention and wishes. This is an argument with further premises, not a consequence established merely by observing regularity.
replacements.3.1.2: Description: Berkeley’s immaterialism challenges material-substance theories using distinctions within empiricist inquiry. Its provocation lies in claiming that ordinary reality can survive the rejection of a philosophical account of matter.
replacements.3.1.15: Impact: Answering recognizable opponents made his position part of existing debates. Attention and controversy do not necessarily imply that his contemporaries accepted or respected every conclusion.
replacements.3.1.17: Description: His Trinity fellowship and later ecclesiastical offices supplied different institutional settings. A deanery is a church office, not an academic post, and the later bishopric should not be made a cause of works he had already published.
replacements.3.1.20: Description: Hume’s response to his account of general ideas and Kant’s efforts to distinguish kinds of idealism show later engagement. Critical rejection can contribute to a philosopher’s reputation as much as adoption.
replacements.3.1.21: Impact: Later debate helped sustain Berkeley’s place in the canon. This explains continuing prominence, not the original formation of arguments that preceded those readers.
replacements.3.2.0: Factors in Berkeley’s Formation and Reception
replacements.3.2.1: The most plausible explanation separates early intellectual formation from later reception. Education, arguments, presentation, and institutional contacts provide mechanisms; calling a thinker a genius does not explain those mechanisms:
replacements.3.2.2: 1. A Radical Challenge: Berkeley combines the denial of material substance with the defense of ordinary sensible objects. That tension created a memorable philosophical alternative. Controversy made it worth answering, even for readers unconvinced by his solution.
replacements.3.2.3: 2. Engagement with Existing Discourse: Berkeley responds to earlier thinkers such as Locke, Descartes, and Malebranche. Hume was born in 1711, after the 1710 Principles appeared, and was a later reader—not Berkeley’s predecessor. Nor should all these opponents be grouped as materialists.
replacements.3.2.4: 3. Argument and Presentation: The Principles develops a connected exposition; the Three Dialogues dramatizes objections and replies through Hylas and Philonous. These different forms give readers more than one route into the argument. Only the latter work has the dialogue format.
replacements.3.2.5: 4. Religious Aims: Berkeley presents his project as opposing skepticism and atheism. Its theological stakes help explain his motivation and audience, but do not establish that religious readers uniformly supported it or that those aims made the argument successful.
replacements.3.2.6: 5. Intellectual Context: Disputes about ideas, matter, causation, and scientific explanation supplied the problems Berkeley addressed. This is more specific than attributing his success to an age being generally receptive to novelty.
replacements.3.2.7: 6. Later Reception: Hume’s explicit acknowledgment and Kant’s critical distinctions kept Berkeley’s arguments in circulation. Such responses help explain his lasting prominence without implying that either later thinker adopted his system.
replacements.3.3.2: Original Argument: Berkeley’s combination of immaterialism, criticism of abstraction, and defense of ordinary experience created a position later readers had to assess. Describing this as genius recognizes achievement but does not independently explain its cause.
replacements.3.3.5: Written Communication: The surviving works show different ways of making an argument accessible, especially the exchanges in the Three Dialogues. A claim about his personal charm is less securely grounded than this observable feature of his writing.
replacements.3.3.6: Ecclesiastical Connections: Church offices and intellectual networks contributed to his later public standing. He became bishop in 1734; the major early works on vision and immaterialism had already appeared, so the bishopric cannot explain their initial composition.
replacements.4.1.6: Impact: Kant explicitly distinguishes his transcendental idealism from Berkeley’s immaterialism. Later idealisms differ over objects, experience, and mind, so their histories should not be reduced to expanding a single claim that minds construct reality.
replacements.4.1.8: Comparison: Berkeley and phenomenologists both examine perception, but do not thereby use the same method or defend the same ontology. Husserl’s suspension of a commitment about existence is not itself Berkeley’s denial of material substance.
replacements.4.1.9: Limit: A direct Berkeley-to-Husserl or Berkeley-to-Merleau-Ponty explanation needs textual evidence. Shared attention to perception alone does not establish the original response’s claimed line of influence.
replacements.4.1.17: Description: Berkeley connects involuntary, ordered sensory experience with divine agency and knowledge. This gives his metaphysics a theological explanation of the world’s independence from any particular finite observer.
replacements.4.1.21: Impact: His account makes the relation between visual signs, touch, movement, and learned expectation a problem for later inquiry. Acceptance of a point about perception does not require acceptance of immaterialism.
replacements.4.1.23: Comparison: Cognitive science also studies how information from different senses supports perception. This offers a useful modern comparison with Berkeley’s vision theory, rather than evidence that the discipline inherits his whole metaphysics.
replacements.4.1.24: Limit: A model in which perception depends on processing does not establish that only ideas and spirits exist. The scientific question about perceptual mechanisms and the metaphysical question about matter remain distinct.
replacements.4.2.1: 1. Empiricism and Epistemology: Berkeley challenges theories of abstract ideas and inaccessible material originals. Hume’s explicit praise of his account of general ideas provides a clear example of reception. Neither thinker’s system is simply a theory that the mind constructs whatever reality it wants.
replacements.4.2.2: 2. Metaphysics and Philosophy of Mind: Berkeley’s ideas-and-spirits distinction offers an alternative to material-substance theories. It raises questions about active agency, passive perception, and other minds. Sensible objects can be independent of my wishes without being independent of every mind in his system.
replacements.4.2.3: 3. Philosophy of Language: His criticism of abstract ideas and his account of general signs address how language can operate without a separate mental picture for every meaningful word. Speech also has practical and affective uses; the source’s purely image-based account was too narrow.
replacements.4.2.4: 4. Cognitive Science and Psychology: His vision theory invites comparison with later work on learned relations between sensory cues. Such comparison must be separated from a documented line of influence and from endorsement of his ontology.
replacements.4.2.5: 5. Later European Idealism: Kant’s critical engagement is especially important, including his efforts to distinguish his position from Berkeley’s. Listing Leibniz and Hume as a simple route into “Continental philosophy” obscures chronology and differences between traditions. The relevant question is how later arguments revise or resist Berkeley’s.
replacements.4.2.6: 6. Theology and Philosophy of Religion: Berkeley’s system appeals to God as an active source of the ordered sensible world, not merely as an extra human observer. Whether his argument establishes that divine role remains a substantive question for critics.
replacements.4.3.5: Philosophy of Mind: The distinction between active spirits and passive ideas sharpens questions about agency and perception. It must not be replaced with a claim that all reality is made of passive mental images.
replacements.4.3.6: Philosophy of Religion: The divine role in the order and continuity of experience connects immaterialism with arguments about God.
replacements.4.3.7: Language and Universals: Berkeley’s criticism of abstract ideas contributes to debates about general signs and meaning. A direct founding role in modern linguistics is not established by that philosophical relevance.
replacements.5.1.0: #1: What is the principal phrase associated with Berkeley’s account of sensible objects?
replacements.5.1.8: #5: What does Berkeley deny when he rejects material substance?
replacements.5.1.9: <details><summary>Answer:</summary> He denies a mind-independent material support behind sensible qualities, while retaining ordinary perceived objects and active spirits.</details>
replacements.5.1.11: <details><summary>Answer:</summary> He rejects indeterminate abstract images, but permits particular ideas and words to represent many cases generally.</details>
replacements.5.2.0: 1: What does “esse est percipi” express in Berkeley’s account of sensible things?
replacements.5.2.1: Their existence consists in being perceived. Active spirits are not passive ideas to which that formula applies in the same way.
replacements.5.2.3: He disputes an unperceived material support for sensible qualities, not every kind of substance; his system retains active spirits.
replacements.5.2.5: Distance is not immediately seen; experience connects visual signs with tangible distance and movement. This need not be a conscious geometrical inference.
replacements.5.2.6: 4: What role does God play in Berkeley’s explanation of ordered sensory experience?
replacements.5.2.7: Divine agency and knowledge sustain an ordered sensible world independent of any one finite observer’s attention and will. The argument requires more than the bare observation of regularity.
replacements.5.2.8: 5: Why does Berkeley reject the claim that every meaningful use of a word must present a distinct idea?
replacements.5.2.9: General signs can represent particulars, and language can prompt action or feeling as well as communicate ideas.
replacements.5.2.11: He tries to remove the gap between perceived things and unknowable material originals. Questions about other spirits and God remain; not every skeptical problem simply disappears.
replacements.5.3.7: <details><summary>Answer:</summary> God supplies, in Berkeley’s account, divine agency and knowledge underlying the order and continuity of the sensible world independently of any particular human observer.</details>
replacements.5.3.9: <details><summary>Answer:</summary> Clear areas of engagement include empiricism, metaphysics, epistemology, perception, philosophy of mind and religion, and philosophical debates about language; this does not establish a direct founding role in modern linguistics.</details>
replacements.5.3.10: #6: How should Berkeley’s later bishopric be related to his early philosophical work?
replacements.5.3.11: <details><summary>Answer:</summary> It contributed to later public standing, but began in 1734, after the major early works; it cannot explain their initial composition.</details>
replacements.6.1.6: Does Berkeley’s “master argument” distinguish adequately between an act of conceiving and the content conceived? How does that affect its support for immaterialism?
replacements.6.1.8: Which specific early modern debates helped make Berkeley’s arguments significant, even for readers who rejected their conclusions?
replacements.6.2.6: How can general words function without distinct abstract images, and how do practical or emotional uses of language complicate a simple word-to-idea model?
replacements.6.2.7: Does rejecting unknowable material originals answer skepticism, or relocate its difficulties to other minds, sensory order, and God?
replacements.6.2.9: What evidence would distinguish direct influence on later theories of perception from a similarity noticed retrospectively?
replacements.6.3.4: How does Berkeley distinguish the existence of sensible objects from that of active spirits, and why does the distinction matter for “to be is to be perceived”?
replacements.6.3.12: Why might philosophers who reject Berkeley’s conclusions still find his arguments important?

highlights: Berkeley denies material substance while defending ordinary sensible objects.
Ideas are passive and perceived; spirits are active perceivers, so the same slogan does not define both.
General thought does not require impossible abstract pictures, and meaningful language need not always summon an idea.
